blocks.text: A geographical perspective on selected issues and problems

Geography studies how people and the environment interact in space. The problems of pollution, waste, urban growth, slums and land degradation are not isolated. They arise where population, economic activity and natural resources meet, and they differ from place to place. A geographical perspective asks four questions about each problem: **where** does it occur, **why** there, **what** are its effects on people and nature, and **how** can it be reduced. This lesson takes five selected issues of India and treats each with its causes, consequences and remedies, in line with NCERT Class 12.
Environmental pollution
The addition of substances or energy to the environment at a rate faster than it can be absorbed, diluted or made harmless, so that it harms living things or the quality of air, water, soil or sound.

**Air pollution** comes from the burning of fossil fuels in vehicles, industries and thermal power plants, from the burning of firewood, crop residue and dung in the open or in households, from dust and construction, and from mining. It causes respiratory and heart diseases, smog, and acid rain, and it harms crops and monuments. Cities with heavy traffic and industries are worst affected, and in winter the cold air near the ground can trap pollutants.

**Water pollution** arises from untreated sewage, industrial effluents, and run-off from farms carrying fertilisers and pesticides. It lowers the dissolved oxygen of the water, kills fish, and spreads diseases such as cholera, typhoid and dysentery. Rivers that pass through large cities and industrial belts, such as the Ganga and the Yamuna, are heavily polluted, which is why programmes such as the Ganga Action Plan were started. Excess nutrients from fertilisers can cause **eutrophication**, an overgrowth of algae that takes the oxygen from water. **Noise pollution** from traffic, industry and loudspeakers causes stress and hearing loss, and **soil pollution** comes from chemicals and solid waste.

The remedies are cleaner fuels and public transport, emission standards, treatment of sewage and effluents before discharge, planting of trees, strict laws, and public awareness. The principle **polluter pays** is applied to make polluters bear the cost of damage.
Urban waste disposal

Cities generate large amounts of **solid waste** such as kitchen waste, paper, plastics, glass, metals, building debris and electronic waste. The amount per person rises with income, and rapid urban growth makes collection and disposal difficult. Open dumping pollutes the land, air and groundwater, breeds flies and rats, and spreads disease, and the liquid that drains from a dump (leachate) contaminates water.

blocks.caption: Methods of solid-waste management
rows: Separates wet (biodegradable) and dry waste at home
All waste; makes other methods possible
Biological decay of organic waste to make manure
Turns used paper, glass, metal and plastic into new products
Dry waste such as paper, metals and glass
Waste is buried in a controlled site with lining, covering and gas and leachate control
The residue that cannot be reused or recycled
Controlled burning that cuts the volume and can produce energy
Combustible waste that is not recyclable

blocks.text: The waste hierarchy is **reduce, reuse, recycle**. Reducing waste at its source is the best option, and disposal is the last resort.

blocks.problem: A city of 2 million people produces 0.5 kg of solid waste per person per day, and 60 per cent of it is compostable. Find the waste generated and the compostable part, in tonnes per day.
blocks.solution: Total waste = 2,000,000 x 0.5 kg = 1,000,000 kg per day. Since 1 tonne = 1,000 kg, this is 1,000 tonnes per day. Compostable part = 60/100 x 1,000 = 600 tonnes per day. The remaining 400 tonnes per day must be recycled, burnt or landfilled.
blocks.answer: 1,000 tonnes per day in total; 600 tonnes per day compostable

blocks.text: Urbanisation and rural-urban migration

**Urbanisation** is the increase in the share of the population living in towns and cities. As per the Census of India definition, a town has a minimum population of 5,000, a density of at least 400 persons per sq km, and at least 75 per cent of its male working population in non-agricultural work, besides places with municipal status. Towns with a population of 1 lakh or more are Class I towns, and cities with 10 lakh or more are called million-plus cities.
The movement of people from villages to towns and cities, driven by push factors in the village and pull factors in the city.

**Push factors** include poverty, unemployment, fragmented small holdings, drought, floods, and the lack of schools and hospitals. **Pull factors** include the chance of jobs and higher incomes, better education and health care, and the attraction of city life. Migration supplies labour to the city and sends money back (remittances), but it makes cities grow faster than houses, water, transport and services can be provided.

blocks.problem: A country has a population of 1,250 million, of whom 400 million live in urban areas. Find its level of urbanisation. If the urban population grows by 10 per cent while the total stays the same, what will the level become?
blocks.solution: Level of urbanisation = urban / total x 100 = 400/1250 x 100 = 32 per cent. A 10 per cent rise gives an urban population of 400 x 1.10 = 440 million. With the total unchanged at 1,250 million, the new level is 440/1250 x 100 = 35.2 per cent.
blocks.answer: 32 per cent now; 35.2 per cent after the rise

blocks.text: Problems of slums
A densely built, overcrowded residential area of poor housing, with little or no water, sanitation, light or open space.

Slums grow where migrants and the urban poor cannot pay the price of land and houses, and where planning has not provided cheap housing. They are found on railway land, along drains and rivers, and on the fringe of the city. Slums are also called jhuggi-jhopri. Their problems are overcrowding, poor ventilation, lack of safe drinking water and toilets, open drains, frequent disease, poor waste collection, fire risk, insecurity of tenure, and in some places crime and social tension. Most slum dwellers work in the informal sector as labourers, vendors and domestic workers, and so are vital to the city.

Solutions include affordable housing, giving secure tenure, providing water, toilets and drains, in-situ upgrading of slums rather than forced removal, creating jobs in villages to reduce distress migration, and planning of cities so that services keep pace with growth.
Land degradation
The decline in the quality and productivity of land due to natural processes and human activity, so that it becomes less useful for farming, grazing or forests.

Degraded land includes **wasteland**, land that is badly eroded, and land affected by salt. The main causes are **deforestation**, **overgrazing**, **unsustainable farming**, shifting cultivation, mining and quarrying, industrial effluents, and heavy and wrong irrigation. In areas of canal irrigation without proper drainage, **waterlogging** raises the water table, brings salts to the surface and causes **salinity and alkalinity**, as in parts of Punjab and Haryana. Water erosion cuts **gullies**, and a badland topography of **ravines** is found in the Chambal region. Wind erosion and the movement of sand affect the margins of the desert.

Remedies include **afforestation** and **shelterbelts** of trees to stop the wind, **contour ploughing and terrace farming** on slopes, **check dams** in gullies, controlled grazing, proper drainage and the use of **gypsum** for alkaline soils, crop rotation and the use of organic manure.

blocks.problem: Of a district of 5,000 sq km, 18 per cent is degraded. Afforestation and soil conservation restore one fifth of the degraded land. Find the area that remains degraded.
blocks.solution: Degraded area = 18/100 x 5,000 = 900 sq km. One fifth of it is restored: 900/5 = 180 sq km. The area still degraded = 900 - 180 = 720 sq km. This is 720/5,000 x 100 = 14.4 per cent of the district.

blocks.text: Revision: air pollution - vehicles, industry, thermal power; water pollution - sewage, effluents, farm run-off; waste hierarchy - reduce, reuse, recycle; push and pull factors drive migration; slums arise from unaffordable land and housing; land degradation - deforestation, overgrazing, waterlogging and salinity; remedies - afforestation, shelterbelts, terracing, check dams, gypsum.

Common mistakes: (1) Treating waterlogging as a drought problem; it is caused by excess irrigation without drainage. (2) Treating all waste as one type; segregation into wet and dry is the first step. (3) Suggesting that removal of slums by force solves the problem. (4) Writing a list of causes without effects and remedies; in a descriptive answer always give cause, effect and remedy. (5) Quoting recent statistics; use only qualitative facts and figures given in the question.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a major source of air pollution in Indian cities?
questions.explanation: Burning of fuel in vehicles, industries and thermal plants releases smoke, gases and particles into the air, and this is a major source of air pollution in cities. Rainwater harvesting, tree planting and composting do not pollute the air and may help the environment.

optionRationale.1: Rainwater harvesting conserves water and does not pollute air.
optionRationale.2: Tree planting helps to reduce air pollution.
optionRationale.4: Composting recycles organic waste and is a waste-management method.

questions.stem: Salinity and alkalinity in irrigated lands are mainly caused by
options: waterlogging due to excess irrigation without drainage
questions.explanation: In canal-irrigated areas without drainage the water table rises, and salts are brought to the surface as the water evaporates. This causes salinity and alkalinity. Tree planting and check dams reduce degradation.

optionRationale.2: Lack of sunshine does not cause salt build-up.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a pull factor of rural-urban migration?
options: Lack of schools in the village
Better job opportunities in the city
questions.explanation: Pull factors are the attractions of the destination, such as better jobs, higher income, education and health care. Drought, small holdings and lack of schools are push factors from the village.

optionRationale.1: Drought is a push factor from the village.
optionRationale.2: Small fragmented holdings are a push factor.
optionRationale.3: Lack of schools in the village is a push factor.

questions.stem: The best way to treat kitchen waste and vegetable peels in a town is
questions.explanation: Kitchen waste is biodegradable and can be turned into manure by composting, which reduces the load on landfills and returns nutrients to the soil. Open burning pollutes air, river dumping pollutes water and mixing with plastic prevents recycling.

optionRationale.3: Dumping in a river causes water pollution.
optionRationale.4: Mixing with plastic prevents recycling and composting.

questions.stem: Match the land-degradation problem in List-I with the remedy in List-II.
questions.explanation: Contour ploughing and terracing control water erosion on slopes. Gypsum is applied to alkaline soils. Shelterbelts check the movement of wind-blown sand at desert margins. Check dams and afforestation are used to control gullies.

optionRationale.2: This swaps remedies for slopes and alkaline soils.
optionRationale.3: This gives the sand-dune problem the contour remedy.
optionRationale.4: This reverses the correct matching almost completely.

left: C. Shifting sand at desert margins

questions.stem: A country has 1,250 million people, of whom 400 million live in urban areas. Its level of urbanisation is
questions.explanation: Level of urbanisation = urban population / total population x 100 = 400 / 1,250 x 100 = 32 per cent. The values 16 and 24 per cent are obtained by wrong division, and 40 per cent mixes numbers.

optionRationale.1: 16 per cent is half the correct value.
optionRationale.2: 24 per cent does not follow from 400/1250.
optionRationale.3: 40 per cent is wrongly taken from the number 400.

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Slums develop in large Indian cities.
Reason (R): Many migrants and the urban poor cannot afford to pay for land and housing in the city.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Land and housing in cities are costly, and many low-income migrants cannot afford them, so they settle in crowded informal housing. This makes the reason a correct explanation of why slums develop.

optionRationale.2: The reason does explain the assertion.
optionRationale.3: The assertion is true, so option 3 is wrong.
optionRationale.4: The assertion is true, so it cannot be false.

questions.objective: Explain the cause of slum growth

questions.stem:
Consider the statements.
A. Overgrazing is a cause of land degradation.
B. Waterlogging may lead to salinity in irrigated areas.
C. Afforestation increases soil erosion.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Overgrazing removes vegetation and exposes soil, and waterlogging brings salts up and causes salinity, so A and B are correct. Afforestation holds the soil with roots and reduces erosion, so C is false.

optionRationale.1: B is also correct, so A alone is incomplete.
optionRationale.2: C is false, so this pair is wrong.
optionRationale.4: C is false, so all three cannot be correct.

questions.stem: As per the Census definition, a settlement is a town if it has at least 5,000 persons, a density of at least 400 persons per sq km and at least 75 per cent of male workers in non-agricultural work. Which settlement qualifies?
questions.explanation: Only the second settlement meets all three conditions: population 8,000 is above 5,000, density 450 is above 400 and 80 per cent is above 75. The first fails on density, the third on population and the fourth on the share of non-agricultural workers.

optionRationale.4: Only 60 per cent male workers are in non-agricultural work, below 75.

questions.objective: Apply the Census definition of a town

questions.stem: A city of 2 million people produces 0.5 kg of waste per person per day, and 60 per cent of it is compostable. The compostable waste, in tonnes per day, is
questions.explanation: Total waste = 2,000,000 x 0.5 = 1,000,000 kg = 1,000 tonnes per day. Compostable waste = 0.60 x 1,000 = 600 tonnes per day. The value 1,000 is the total and 400 is the non-compostable part.

optionRationale.3: 1,000 tonnes is the total waste, not the compostable part.

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Excessive irrigation without drainage can cause salinity in the soil.
Reason (R): The salts brought by irrigation water move down and are washed away completely.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The assertion is true: when the water table rises, the water evaporates and the dissolved salts are left at the surface. The reason is false because, without drainage, salts accumulate and are not washed away.

optionRationale.1: The reason is false, so it cannot explain the assertion.
optionRationale.2: The reason is false, so both cannot be true.
optionRationale.4: The assertion is true, so (A) is not false.

questions.stem: A city has 4 million people, 25 per cent of them in slums. After a decade the city has 4.8 million people and the slum population has risen by 40 per cent. The slum share of the population is now nearest to
questions.explanation: Initial slum population = 0.25 x 4 million = 1 million. A 40 per cent rise gives 1.4 million. The new share = 1.4 / 4.8 x 100 = 29.2 per cent, nearest to 29 per cent. The slum population grew faster than the total, so the share rose.

optionRationale.1: 25 per cent is the share at the start.
optionRationale.3: 35 per cent would need a slum population of 1.68 million.
optionRationale.4: 40 per cent is the rate of growth, not the share.

questions.stem:
Consider the statements on solid-waste management.
A. Segregation of wet and dry waste at source helps recycling.
B. Open dumping is safe and causes no pollution.
C. A sanitary landfill is a controlled site with measures against leachate and gas.
D. Incineration reduces the volume of waste and can produce energy.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Segregation, sanitary landfills and incineration are recognised methods and have the properties stated, so A, C and D are correct. B is false, because open dumps pollute land, air and groundwater and spread disease.

optionRationale.1: B is false, so this pair is wrong.
optionRationale.2: B is false, so this set is wrong.
optionRationale.3: C is also correct, so this pair is incomplete.

questions.stem: Afforestation reduces land degradation mainly because
options: roots bind the soil and the canopy softens the impact of rain
trees increase the speed of surface run-off
trees make the soil more saline
trees dry up all the groundwater
questions.explanation: Roots hold the soil particles together, leaves and litter protect the surface from the impact of raindrops, and the cover slows run-off, so erosion is reduced. Trees do not increase run-off or salinity, and they do not dry up all groundwater.

optionRationale.2: Trees slow, not speed up, run-off.
optionRationale.4: Trees do not remove all groundwater.

questions.stem: Rapid unplanned urban growth fed by rural-urban migration is most likely to result in
options: shortage of housing and growth of slums
a fall in demand for urban jobs
excess of water and sanitation facilities
questions.explanation: When migrants arrive faster than houses and services are built, housing and services fall short and slums grow, with traffic congestion and pressure on water. It does not reduce demand for jobs or give excess facilities.

optionRationale.2: Migration raises, not lowers, the demand for jobs.

questions.objective: Predict the effects of unplanned urban growth
